title: Help
intro: How CentralDungeon works and how each part is used. It grows with the application: what is here is what you can already do today.

search.title: How to search
search.intro: The site's search boxes understand a short language, the same one everywhere. You can type a name and be done; the rest is for when you want to narrow things down.
search.plain: Typing text searches by that box's basic criterion. In the people search, the Discord name or the display name.
search.field: The slash opens the list of fields. You pick with the arrows and confirm with Enter or Tab. The field stays as a fixed chip, and everything you type after it is its value, spaces included.
search.commas: Commas separate alternatives of the same criterion: any one of them is enough.
search.connectors: “/or” and “/and” close the criterion and join the next one, leaving their own chip in between. Tap that chip to switch from one to the other.
search.onlySlash: The slash is the only separator. An “and” or an “or” typed without one is part of what you are searching for, not an instruction.
search.order: Criteria apply in the order they appear, left to right, with no hidden precedence rules.
search.chips: Each chip is removed with its ×. With the text empty, Backspace undoes the last step: first it releases the open field, then it hands the last chip back to the cursor so you can edit it.
search.debounce: There is nothing to press: the search runs on its own when you stop typing.
search.example1: People whose Discord name or display name contains “damian”.
search.example2: The same, but only by display name.
search.example3: Any of the three, by display name.
search.example4: People matching one criterion or the other.
search.example5: Only the ones matching both at once.

steps.step1: Type what you are looking for and wait a second: the list updates on its own, with nothing to press.
steps.step2: If there are too many results, type / and pick the field with the arrows. The chip stays fixed and everything you keep typing is its value.
steps.step3: If any of several options of the same field will do, separate them with commas: damian,carlos,daniel.
steps.step4: To add another criterion, type /or or /and, pick it from the list, and carry on with the next one.
steps.step5: To fix things: tap a chip's ×, tap the connector chip to swap “and” for “or”, or press Backspace on the empty text.

contexts.title: The contexts
contexts.intro: Roles stack: you can be a player and a master at once. Admin and owner are the exception, because they are the same role with a different reach: you hold one of the two. Top left there is a selector that switches context and the screens with it. It is how the interface is organized, not a permission: what you may do is decided by the server on every action.
contexts.player: You browse the open tables, apply to them, and follow your applications and your tables.
contexts.master: You run tables. It appears if you hold the role or if you are a master of at least one table even without it: running a table and being able to create your own are different things.
contexts.admin: You review the tables waiting for approval, request changes, and create tables without a master to assign one later.
contexts.owner: An admin with more reach: everything an admin does, plus auditing, files and account migration once those are built. It does not stack with admin, it replaces it.

steps.step1: Tap the context selector, top left, next to the site name.
steps.step2: Pick the context you want to work in. Only the ones that apply to you are listed.
steps.step3: The screens change with the context; your notifications and your account do not, they are always there.

account.title: Your account
account.login: You sign in with Discord and you have to be a member of the community server. There is no separate sign-up and no password.
account.onboarding: The first time, two things are asked: the name to show and your country. You cannot go on until they are filled in.
account.theme: From the avatar menu you switch between light and dark theme, pick the language, and sign out. The first time, the language comes from your browser; when that cannot be worked out it stays in Spanish. Whatever you pick is remembered.

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.what: The bell at the top collects what happened to you: a new application on your table, a decision about yours.
notifications.click: Tapping a notification takes you where it happened, switching context on its own if it has to.
notifications.history: The full history is on the notifications screen, and that is where they get marked as read.

tableStatus.title: A table's statuses
tableStatus.intro: Almost everything you can do with a table depends on the status it is in, which is why it is always shown.
tableStatus.Unassigned: An admin created it and it has no master yet. It opens on its own as soon as it gets one.
tableStatus.Preparation: The master is putting it together, or has already sent it for review.
tableStatus.ChangesRequested: An admin asked for corrections before approving it.
tableStatus.Opened: It is published: it can be seen and applied to.
tableStatus.PauseRequested: The master asked to pause it and is waiting for an answer.
tableStatus.Pause: It is frozen; it can be resumed.
tableStatus.Finished: It ended the way it was meant to.
tableStatus.Canceled: It was cut short, with a reason on the record.

applying.title: Applying to a table
applying.where: From the explorer you open an open table's detail and apply there, with an optional message for the master.
applying.oneAtATime: You cannot have two active applications to the same table, and you cannot apply to a table you run.
applying.blocked: If the table is full or not open, instead of a greyed-out button you get the reason in writing.

steps.step1: From the explorer, open the table you are interested in and read its description and requirements.
steps.step2: Tap “Apply”. If the button is not there, you will read the reason in its place.
steps.step3: Write a message for the master if you want to tell them something. It is optional.
steps.step4: Send it and follow the application from “My applications”: that is where you see the master's decision.

applicationStatus.title: Where your application stands
applicationStatus.intro: You follow all of them from “My applications”.
applicationStatus.Candidate: The master has not decided yet.
applicationStatus.Player: You were accepted: the table now shows up under “My tables”.
applicationStatus.Rejected: The master turned it down with a written reason. You can apply again later.
applicationStatus.auto: If the table fills up, the applications left without a seat are rejected on their own.

myTables.title: Your tables
myTables.list: “My tables” shows the ones you were accepted into and that are still alive.
myTables.status: Each one carries its status in plain sight: while it is paused or in preparation there is nothing to do, and it says so.

scheduleConflict.title: Schedule clashes
scheduleConflict.local: Tables show their agenda in your own time, even though it is stored in UTC underneath.
scheduleConflict.blocked: You cannot apply to a table that clashes with another one you already play at. The table tells you, and names which one.
scheduleConflict.candidate: Having several pending applications that clash is fine: until you are accepted into one there is no commitment.
scheduleConflict.notified: When you are accepted into one, if any of your other applications now clashes with it, you get a notice. Nobody rejects them for you.
scheduleConflict.withdraw: You can withdraw a pending application from “My applications”. Once accepted you cannot: that is a conversation with the master.

steps.step2: Find the pending application you want to let go of.
steps.step3: Tap “Withdraw” and confirm. If you change your mind later, you have to apply again.

mySessions.title: My sessions and my attendance
mySessions.where: Go to “My tables” and tap the table: its agenda, the full calendar and your attendance are all there.
mySessions.local: Every date is shown in your own time, even though the system stores them in UTC. The footer says which zone you are seeing them in.
mySessions.paused: If the table is paused, the pending sessions are not shown: there is no date to promise until it resumes.
mySessions.cancelled: A cancelled session stays in sight with its number, and the table adds another one at the end: you still play the same number.
mySessions.threeNumbers: Your attendance is three numbers and not a percentage: present, excused and absent. Missing after warning and simply not turning up are different things, and an average would hide that.
mySessions.denominator: The denominator is the sessions with something recorded. The ones nobody has marked yet do not count: if they did, a table that just started would make you look like a chronic absentee.
mySessions.notKarma: Attendance does not go into your karma. It is shown separately, because they are two different signals and mixing them would make the number impossible to explain.

steps.step2: Tap the table you care about.
steps.step3: Look at “My sessions” for the calendar and “My attendance” for the three numbers.

creating.title: Creating a table
creating.role: Creating your own tables needs the Master role. Running a table you were assigned does not: they are different things.
creating.wizard: The wizard runs in four steps: identity, catalogs, agenda and seats. The last one shows you the summary before sending.
creating.submit: When it is ready it goes to an admin for review.

steps.step1: Switch to the Master context with the selector at the top.
steps.step2: Go to “My tables” and tap “Create table”.
steps.step3: Follow the four steps. The table is born in preparation and nobody can see it yet.
steps.step4: When it is ready, send it for review from the Status tab.
steps.step5: Wait for an admin's decision: the bell tells you. If they ask for changes, it arrives with the reason in writing.

schedule.title: Agenda and schedules
schedule.local: Times are typed in your own zone and stored in UTC. The editor shows you both: if the day shifts, that is expected.
schedule.duration: The length is of one session, not of the campaign. It is what decides how late each slot runs.
schedule.interval: Two tables clash if they overlap, not only if they start at the same time: a three-hour one at 20:00 overlaps another at 22:00.
schedule.chained: Chaining two tables is fine: one that starts exactly when the other ends does not clash.
schedule.conflict: You cannot run two live tables that overlap. If you try to save an agenda like that, the system tells you which one it clashes with.
schedule.paused: A paused table does not reserve its slot: its agenda is frozen. It is checked again when you resume it.
schedule.players: If you move the agenda of a table that already has people, anybody it now clashes for gets a notice. Nobody is dropped over it: the system informs, people decide.

steps.step1: On the wizard's “Agenda” step, set the date of the first session and how long one session lasts.
steps.step2: Add one slot per day the table plays, with the day and the time in your own zone.
steps.step3: Look at the “In UTC” line of each slot: that is what gets stored.
steps.step4: If a clash comes up when you save, change the time or free up the other table.

sessions.title: Your table's sessions
sessions.materialize: The calendar builds itself when an admin approves the table: it takes the start date, the weekly agenda and the number of sessions, and creates one row per session with its number.
sessions.missing: If any of the three is missing, the table opens anyway but with no calendar. Fill in what is missing and the sessions appear; nobody blocks the approval over it.
sessions.local: Dates are stored in UTC and shown in your own time. Below the field it says which zone you are typing in.
sessions.correct: You can correct the date of a single session. It is a correction to that evening and does not change the table's weekly agenda.
sessions.notes: Each session's notes are yours: no player sees them.
sessions.hold: Marking a session as played is a separate action from recording attendance. The system does not infer one from the other: you can record who came without closing it, and close it without recording anybody.
sessions.cancel: When you cancel a session, the table adds another one at the end of the calendar, on the next free slot of your agenda. That way you still play the number you promised; what moves is the closing date.
sessions.cancelRecord: The cancelled session does not disappear: it keeps its number as the record that it was planned. The players are notified.
sessions.locked: A session already played or cancelled is not edited: it is the record of something that happened, or that did not.
sessions.paused: While the table is paused no dates are promised: the pending sessions are hidden, from you as well. When you resume it they are scheduled again from that day, keeping their numbering.
sessions.resumeConflict: If while it was paused you took on another table that overlaps this one, it cannot be resumed until you fix one of the two agendas. A paused table does not reserve its slot, and on the way back it claims it.
sessions.attendance: Attendance is recorded per session, with four values: present, excused, absent and not recorded. The roster is the table's accepted players.

steps.step1: Open your table from “My tables” as a master and go to the “Sessions” tab.
steps.step2: Tap a session to expand it: its date, its notes and its roster are all there.
steps.step3: Correct the date or write the notes and tap “Save changes”.
steps.step4: Pick each player's attendance and tap “Save attendance”.
steps.step5: Once the session has happened, mark it as played with the ✓ in the header. If it did not happen, cancel it with the ✗ — it warns you before confirming that another one is added at the end.

review.title: Review and changes
review.approve: If an admin approves it, the table opens and applications start coming in.
review.changes: If they ask for changes, it arrives with the reason in writing: you fix it and send it back.
review.history: Every transition is recorded on the Status tab, with who made it and why.

candidates.title: Candidates
candidates.order: They are ordered by application date and that order is never re-sorted.
candidates.accept: Accepting adds the person to the table. If that fills it, the remaining applications are rejected on their own.
candidates.reject: Rejecting asks for a reason and cannot be undone, but the person can apply again.

steps.step1: Open your table and go to the Candidates tab.
steps.step2: Read each person's message. The order is by application date.
steps.step3: Tap “Accept” to add them to the table, or “Reject” and write the reason.
steps.step4: If accepting fills the table, the remaining applications are rejected on their own.

running.title: Running the table
running.start: Starting it moves it to “In progress”. Finishing closes it as ended.
running.cancel: Cancelling cuts the table short and asks for a written reason. An admin can do it too.
running.who: Starting, finishing and cancelling belong to the table's master; a co-master does not see them.

steps.step1: Open your table and go to the Status tab.
steps.step2: Tap “Start table” when they begin playing: it moves to “In progress”.
steps.step3: When it ends, “Finish table”. If it has to be cut short, “Cancel table” and write the reason.
steps.step4: Every change stays in that tab's history, with who made it and why.

coMasters.title: Master and co-masters
coMasters.one: Every table has one master and can have co-masters.
coMasters.primary: The master is the one who decides about the table; co-masters help run it.
coMasters.assign: When an admin assigns masters, the first one they add is the master and the rest become co-masters.

deleting.title: When a table is not going to happen
deleting.draft: If it was never published — in preparation or with changes requested — and nobody applied, it is deleted: nobody saw it, so there is nothing to tell.
deleting.public: If it was already open, in progress or paused, it is not deleted: it is cancelled with a written reason. Other people saw it or played at it, and that is history.
deleting.gone: Deleting is final and leaves no public trace: the table disappears from your tables and from everywhere. Cancelling leaves it visible as cancelled.

steps.step1: Open the table and go to the Status tab.
steps.step2: If it has not been published yet you will see “Delete table” next to “Cancel table”.
steps.step3: Confirm. If the table had already opened, the button is not there: cancelling is the right thing then.

proposeCatalog.title: Proposing a system, tag or platform
proposeCatalog.what: When you put a table together you pick its systems, tags and platforms from a list. If the one you want is not there, you can propose it from the same field.
proposeCatalog.pending: You can use it on your table right away, but it stays pending approval: until an admin accepts it, nobody else sees it and nobody can filter by it.
proposeCatalog.marked: While it is pending it shows up marked as such on your table, so you know why nobody else can see it.
proposeCatalog.existing: If what you were about to propose already exists spelled differently, pick the one that is there: the search finds the table under either name once an admin joins them.

steps.step1: In the system, tag or platform field, type what you are looking for.
steps.step2: If it shows up in the list, pick it.
steps.step3: If it does not, tap “Propose” with the name you typed.
steps.step4: Carry on building the table: you do not have to wait for approval to publish it.

reviewing.title: Reviewing tables
reviewing.queue: “Tables to review” collects the ones waiting on a decision: those in preparation and those without a master yet.
reviewing.approve: Approving publishes the table. Requesting changes sends it back to the master with the reason in writing.
reviewing.gone: Once approved, the table leaves the queue: the queue is what is pending, not a listing of everything.

steps.step1: Switch to the Admin context and go to “Tables to review”.
steps.step2: Open the table you want to review and read what the master prepared.
steps.step3: Tap “Approve” to publish it, or “Request changes” and write what has to be fixed.
steps.step4: The table leaves the queue: the queue is what is pending, not a listing of everything.

assignMasters.title: Tables without a master
assignMasters.create: An admin can create a table without being its master. It is born unassigned and is not published until it has one.
assignMasters.search: To assign it you search for people by Discord name or display name, with the same search language as everywhere else.
assignMasters.order: The first one you add is the master and the rest become co-masters. Tap a name to make them the master: the previous one becomes a co-master.
assignMasters.opens: On assigning, the table opens directly, without going through review.

steps.step1: In “Tables to review”, tap “Create table without a master” and give it a name.
steps.step2: On that table's row, tap “Assign masters”.
steps.step3: Search for the person by Discord name or display name and tap their name in the list.
steps.step4: Add the others the same way. The first is the master; the rest become co-masters.
steps.step5: If you want a different master, tap their name in the chips: the previous one becomes a co-master.
steps.step6: Tap “Assign masters”. The table opens immediately, without going through review.

assignMasters.delete: If the unassigned table is not going to happen after all, it is deleted from that same row: it was never published, so no trace is left.

owner.title: Owner
owner.same: An owner can do everything an admin can: it is the same role with more reach.
owner.soon: What is theirs alone — auditing, deleting files and migrating accounts — is still being built, and this help will explain it once it exists.
owner.exclusive: That is why nobody is an admin and an owner at once: you hold one of the two, and owner is the one above.

catalogs.title: Catalogs: systems, tags and platforms
catalogs.what: A catalog is the list of values masters can pick from when putting a table together. Masters can also propose a new one, and that is where you come in.
catalogs.pending: A proposed value stays pending: the master can already use it on their table, but players neither see it nor can filter by it until you accept it.
catalogs.groups: When you accept it you decide whether it is a new value or another way of writing one that already exists. The second builds a group: “DANDD” and “D&D 5e” become the same value as far as searching goes.
catalogs.alias: Each table still shows the name its own master picked. The equivalence works in the search, not on the screen.
catalogs.merge: Merging joins two groups; splitting takes a value out of its group. Neither touches the tables: whatever was already tagged is still found the same way.
catalogs.disable: Disabling takes a value out of circulation without breaking anything. The tables using it keep it, and restoring it brings everything back as it was.
catalogs.successor: If you disable the main value of a group, you pick which of its equivalents becomes the main one. The system does not decide it on its own.

steps.step1: Switch to the Admin context and go to “Catalogs”.
steps.step2: Pick the tab of the catalog you want to review: systems, tags or platforms.
steps.step3: Search by name if the list is long.
steps.step4: On a pending value, tap “Accept” and decide whether it is new or belongs to an existing group.
steps.step5: To join two groups, tap “Merge” on the one you want to stop existing and pick the one that stays.
steps.step6: To take a value out of circulation, tap “Disable”. If it is a group's main one, pick who replaces it.
